## Four voices, one question

Our talk is planned for **6 minutes 48 seconds**, including handovers, pointing and pauses. Slides 1–10 carry the talk. Slide 11 stays on screen for questions. Allow roughly two minutes for questions within the group's ten-minute slot. These are rehearsal targets. Time a full run together.

| Speaker | Slides | Clock when handing over | What the audience should understand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1–2 | 1:25 | Who is in the data and what was recorded. |
| 2 | 3–4 | 2:57 | What the model knows on the day a student enrols. |
| 3 | 5–7 | 4:48 | How many the rule catches and what the warnings cost in staff time. |
| 4 | 8–10 | 6:48 | Why a smaller gap can still leave both groups worse off on missed warnings. |

## Slide 11: Sources and acknowledgements

Keep this slide available during questions. The group can show the original data description, the two Data to Viz entries on boxplots and interval labels, and the report's tool disclosure. Speaker 4 can take the first question about group errors. When another speaker has the relevant evidence, invite them in.

For example, when asked why the thresholds have the same AUC, explain that both thresholds act on exactly the same ranking of the 889 test students. When asked about uncertainty, identify what was resampled and what was held fixed. The separate question bank has the counts and longer answers.
